title: The Hidden Jeopardy of Expected Rewards
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that most workplace rewards quietly become 'expected' the moment they are repeated a second time, and that expected rewards lose nearly all of their motivational power. The real danger, the author explains, isn't in giving them but in what happens the rare time they don't materialize -- an absence that gets remembered far longer than the reward itself ever motivated anyone. The piece draws a parallel to birthdays and holiday gifts to make the psychological stakes concrete. Its practical advice for leaders is simple: never repeat the same reward twice in a row, even a popular one, so it never calcifies into an entitlement. Avoiding that trap, the author argues, protects the reward's power over the long run.
points: Any reward repeated two or more times becomes an expected, calculated reward that loses most of its motivational force.
Expected rewards matter most, and hurt most, in the rare instance when they fail to occur.
The absence of an expected reward is read as a sign of being forgotten or unimportant.
Leaders should mix and vary rewards rather than repeating the same one in succession.
quotes: In fact, any time a leader or organization repeats a reward two times or more, it becomes an expected or calculated reward.
The only time an expected reward really matters over time is when it doesn’t happen. Then, it is remembered forever.
Expected rewards that don’t occur carry a deep symbolic meaning to people.
The key is to remember not to repeat a reward, no matter its popularity, twice in a row.
Expected or calculated rewards are the enemy of great leadership. The idea is not to create them in the first place.
